claims.text: The as-synthesized nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs catalyst is a solid solution with a near-random atomic distribution.
A suitable probe molecule can preferentially adsorb on surface Rh sites in PtPdRhRuIrOs.
Potential cycling can induce Rh segregation in PtPdRhRuIrOs.
Preferential probe adsorption or potential cycling will reduce the prevalence of Rh-rich surface ensembles.
The proposed modification shifts the distribution of surface near-neighbor configurations toward fewer Rh-rich ensembles.
The atomic surroundings of an active site in a multicomponent catalyst can tune that site's electronic properties.
Composition, strain, and diverse local coordination can regulate distributions of adsorption energies on high-entropy-alloy surfaces.
Selective modification of Rh sites changes the local electronic and geometric configurations of PtPdRhRuIrOs.
The resulting local configurations change the adsorption energies of key oxygenated ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Reducing Rh-rich ensembles suppresses undesired over-oxidation pathways and favors desired ethanol-oxidation pathways.
Compared with an untreated catalyst, the modified catalyst will have higher selectivity toward acetaldehyde or acetic acid.
Compared with the untreated catalyst, the modified catalyst will produce fewer over-oxidized byproducts.
The untreated baseline retains a near-random distribution of active sites during ethanol oxidation.
Large changes in potential, temperature, or electrolyte composition may alter the proposed selectivity effect.

contradictions.description: Potential cycling is said to induce Rh segregation while also reducing Rh-rich domains or ensembles. Segregation ordinarily denotes enrichment or clustering, so the stated intervention and mediator point in opposing structural directions unless a more specific dealloying or subsurface-segregation process is defined.

Preferential probe adsorption would primarily block or chemically modify existing Rh sites, whereas the mediator and characterization plan describe a change in the atomic distribution of Rh-rich ensembles. Site blocking does not by itself imply atomic redistribution.
